items.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
items.summary: The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October, the highest outside of the pandemic period in a decade.
items.body: Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly. The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis. About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed " and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021. "This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform.

items.title: The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%
items.summary: Coreweave's steep yields reflect stress in the AI debt markets as investors worry about a data center slowdown. What comes next.
items.body: Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit. That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away." That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress. The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave . The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank.

items.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
items.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
items.body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday. Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development. However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September. On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

items.title: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph
items.summary: Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier. A sell-off…
items.body: European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier. A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March. The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened. Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.

items.title: Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck
items.summary: Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.
items.body: Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year. The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis. "Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site. The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections , where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

items.title: ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026
items.body: The European Central Bank (ECB) has published consolidated banking data as at end-June 2026 , a dataset for the EU banking system compiled on a group consolidated basis. The quarterly data provide information required to analyse the EU banking sector and comprise a subset of the information that is available in the year-end dataset. The data cover 336 banking groups and 2283 stand-alone credit institutions and non-EU controlled subsidiaries and branches operating in the EU, accounting for nearly 100% of the EU banking sector’s balance sheet. They include an extensive range of indicators on profitability and efficiency, balance sheet composition, liquidity and funding, asset quality, asset encumbrance, capital adequacy and solvency. Aggregates and indicators are published for the reporting population.

items.title: Beijing calls for more efforts to stabilise stock market after renewed sell-off
items.summary: China’s State Council has pledged improved policy mechanisms to stabilise the country’s struggling stock market, after stocks slid again on Friday following a meltdown on the US markets. “We will enhance the inherent stability of the stock market and foster the steady and…
items.body: China’s State Council has pledged improved policy mechanisms to stabilise the country’s struggling stock market, after stocks slid again on Friday following a meltdown on the US markets. “We will enhance the inherent stability of the stock market and foster the steady and healthy development of the capital market,” officials at the State Council executive meeting, chaired by Chinese Premier Li Qiang, were quoted as saying on Friday. The comments came as the CSI 300 Index, which tracks major Chinese firms traded in Shanghai and Shenzhen, sank 1.4 per cent on Friday, following the market collapse in the United States. Technology stocks led the drop, with the Star 50 gauge – which has large exposure to AI chipmakers trading in Shanghai – slumping 2.6 per cent.

items.title: Investors brace for lower Anthropic valuation, calling $1.5 trillion a 'stretch'
items.summary: Anthropic could list below a $1.5 trillion valuation, trailing previous expectations, as the AI trade sours on Wall Street.
items.body: Following tech's selloff on Wall Street this week, some investors are lowering their expectations for Anthropic. The artificial intelligence company had been looking toward a $2 trillion valuation in its IPO up until recently, but stakeholders told CNBC that even $1.5 trillion is now in doubt, with one investor calling that number a "stretch." The change in sentiment comes alongside growing concerns about the outsized spending by AI companies and a sharp post-midterm slump in the market. The Nasdaq plummeted more than 5% on Thursday, its steepest drop in 19 months, reflecting fears that Democrats' newfound power in Washington, D.C., and a nationwide rebuke of AI will lead to a slowdown in the buildout of data centers. Bearishness on the AI trade was on the rise before the election.

items.body: PARIS -- Weak car-buyer demand in China is driving more of the country's electric vehicle makers into Europe, with Seres Group and Li Auto preparing for their debuts on the continent in 2027.

items.title: U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October, way more than expected; unemployment rate slips to 4.1%
items.summary: Nonfarm payrolls were expected to increase by 59,000 in October as the unemployment rate was expected to hold steady at 4.2%.
items.body: The U.S. economy added jobs at a much stronger-than-expected pace in October, while the unemployment rate moved lower as the labor market showed surprising strength. Nonfarm payrolls increased by a seasonally adjusted 165,000 for the month, compared with the Dow Jones estimate for 59,000, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. The unemployment rate nudged down to 4.1%, compared with the forecast for 4.2%. A more encompassing measure that includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons rose to 7.9%, up 0.3 percentage point, amid an increase of 421,000 in the civilian labor force. In addition to the strong payroll gains for October, prior months were revised up substantially: The August figure moved to 186,000, an upward revision of 53,000, while the September count shifted to 60,000 following an upward revision of 31,000.

items.title: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff
items.summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
items.body: Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check? That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets. The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple. It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress. A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence. Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

items.title: UK dairy farmers face further pressure as milk processor cuts prices
items.summary: Freshways lowers price paid to producers by 7p a litre, prompting warnings confidence in the sector is ‘at rock bottom’ “Milk is leaving the farm at a loss,” says dairy farmer Ian Harvey, as he warns confidence in the sector is “at rock bottom”. Most of the UK’s dairy producers…
items.body: “Milk is leaving the farm at a loss,” says dairy farmer Ian Harvey, as he warns confidence in the sector is “at rock bottom”. Most of the UK’s dairy producers were already being paid less for their milk than it costs to produce it after a year of volatile farmgate milk prices, combined with the impact of the summer’s drought and soaring costs of vital fuel and fertiliser triggered by the conflict in Iran. However, the industry has been shaken further by the decision by two large milk processors in recent days to cut the price they pay farmers for their liquid milk. Freshways, a big processor that supplies bottles of milk to corner shops, cafes, hotels and wholesalers, announced it was slashing the price it pays for milk by 7p a litre from 1 December, reducing it to 29.4p a litre. The company blamed weaker dairy markets and said poor returns for liquid milk were squeezing processors.

items.title: Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability
items.summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
items.body: Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament. If, in response to nationwide protests , the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have. France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense. Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating . France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency.

items.title: After midterms upheaval, US ag exporters call for stability in China trade
items.summary: As the midterm “blue wave” threatens to further complicate US-China relations, American agricultural exporters are calling on Washington to focus on delivering the trade deals already agreed with Beijing and ending a period of damaging policy uncertainty. With shipments of key…
items.body: As the midterm “blue wave” threatens to further complicate US-China relations, American agricultural exporters are calling on Washington to focus on delivering the trade deals already agreed with Beijing and ending a period of damaging policy uncertainty. With shipments of key products such as soybeans needing to be planned months – or sometimes an entire year – ahead, US farmers are in need of stability after last year’s trade war. “Agriculture is ... an industry with long production cycles, so many things need to be planned well in advance,” said Frank Zhou, managing director of Cargill China, the Chinese arm of US agribusiness group Cargill.

items.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty
items.summary: Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan is charged with planting a recording device in a conference room at artificial intelligence giant OpenAI.
items.body: The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court. Abdulrahman Alfozan , 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case. A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show. Prosecutors say that he put a recording device in a television in an executive conference room at OpenAI's offices in San Francisco on Sept. 28. Alfozan's lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang. Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm, Raed Ventures .

items.title: How does it affect me if share prices fall?
items.summary: Changes in the FTSE 100 and other indexes are not just for financial experts, they can affect our lives.
items.body: Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections. The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years. As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange. Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant. Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends. Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.

items.title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
items.summary: Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices. The latest…
items.body: A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices. The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria , Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK. Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally. The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers. A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.

items.title: European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets
items.summary: European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.
items.body: European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe. Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress. The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines. European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks. Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

items.title: Ahead of Shenzhen trade talks, US holds off blacklist rule that angered Beijing
items.summary: Ahead of a new round of bilateral trade talks, the US has extended the suspension of an expanded trade blacklist that helped inflame tensions with China last year and could subject overseas subsidiaries of Chinese companies to greater scrutiny. The US Bureau of Industry and…
items.body: Ahead of a new round of bilateral trade talks, the US has extended the suspension of an expanded trade blacklist that helped inflame tensions with China last year and could subject overseas subsidiaries of Chinese companies to greater scrutiny. The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a final rule on Thursday extending the suspension of its 50 per cent affiliate rule until January 10, when the current US-China trade truce is also set to expire. If implemented, the measure would extend US restrictions to any company that is at least 50 per cent owned by firms on the US Entity List or Military End-User List, which include organisations that Washington considers national security risks. The suspension was originally agreed by Washington and Beijing following a meeting between their leaders in South Korea late last year and had been due to expire on Monday.

items.title: Hoax bomb threats repeatedly disrupt flights across Europe this week. Here’s what we know
items.summary: Dozens of flights across Europe reported bomb threats this week, disrupting air travel across London, Dublin, and Helsinki.
items.body: Flights across Europe were repeatedly targeted by "hoax" bomb threats this week, disrupting air travel across London, Copenhagen, Dublin, and Helsinki. Danish police were investigating threats to air traffic at Copenhagen airport on Friday but did not find any immediate danger to passengers, according to reports from Reuters. "We are once again at Copenhagen Airport today in connection with threats directed at air traffic," police said in a statement, per Reuters. "We are now investigating the incident and have a visible presence at the airport." Meanwhile, Czech police also said Friday that there were threats to planes departing from and landing in Prague. At least 27 different flights were impacted on Thursday, according to Reuters , with some forced to land unexpectedly and others escorted by fighter jets.

items.title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
items.summary: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.
items.body: The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU. The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe. Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month. But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era. Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.

items.title: Dream ticket? Super-rich can sleep pretty with Singapore Airlines ‘largest double bed in the sky’
items.summary: Cabin upgrade comes as airlines compete for wealthy customers in race to the top of luxury travel Singapore Airlines has said it will offer the “largest double bed in the sky” as part of a S$2bn (£1.2bn) cabin upgrade as super-rich passengers demand ever greater levels of luxury…
items.body: Singapore Airlines has said it will offer the “largest double bed in the sky” as part of a S$2bn (£1.2bn) cabin upgrade as super-rich passengers demand ever greater levels of luxury travel. The first-class premium cabins will feature what the airline claims is “the largest double bed in commercial aviation”. The bed for two people travelling together spans two adjoining seats and measures 203cm (80in) long and 152cm (60in) wide. A standard double bed mattress in the UK is 190cm long and 135cm wide. The bed will include a mattress topper from the German luxury bedding company Paradies, a duvet and a choice of pillows. Some business-class seats would be able to be made into a double bed, the airline said. The upgrade includes curved sliding doors to give passengers more privacy and ultra-high-definition 4K touchscreens.

items.title: China’s skyscraper expertise earns Shenzhen a place on global watch list
items.summary: China’s construction expertise has gained fresh international recognition, with Shenzhen named among the top cities to watch for high-rise development in 2027 by a UK industry publication. A skyscraper originally planned as the headquarters of failed property giant China…
items.body: China’s construction expertise has gained fresh international recognition, with Shenzhen named among the top cities to watch for high-rise development in 2027 by a UK industry publication. A skyscraper originally planned as the headquarters of failed property giant China Evergrande Group was among the projects highlighted. London Construction Magazine included Shenzhen in its “Global Tall Building Construction 2027: Ten Cities to Watch” list on Thursday, citing the city’s experience building complex skyscrapers, its specialist engineering capabilities and its growing role in international collaboration. One project highlighted was the Shenzhen Bay Financial Centre Tower, which is scheduled for completion in 2029. The tower is expected to stand at about 394 metres (1,292 feet), with more than 80 floors and 75 lifts.

items.title: Microsoft plans to use fewer neoclouds as AI buildout shows signs of strain
items.summary: Microsoft is winding down the number of neoclouds it counts as partners, picking key suppliers and focusing on its own data centers.
items.body: Microsoft is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners as it focuses on work with a few key suppliers and builds out its own data centers, according to people familiar with the matter. The software giant's plans pose another potential challenge for a corner of the artificial intelligence market that's showing signs of strain due to rising borrowing costs, hefty debt loads and concerns about whether the buildout will slow down. Microsoft has forged relationships in recent years with a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave , Nebius, Chronoscale , IREN , Lambda and Nscale, as well as with Oracle , which is pouring money into building out AI infrastructure. Microsoft is now in the evaluation stage and hasn't decided which neoclouds it will stop using, said two sources, who asked not to be named because the talks are confidential.

items.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
items.summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
items.body: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says. He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars. But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab." With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since. Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

items.title: Commuters and shoppers face disruption from tube driver strikes in run-up to Christmas
items.summary: RMT union calls eight 24-hour strikes on London Underground in opposition to plans for four-day week Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – including six in the lead-up to Christmas – that threaten to bring transport chaos to…
items.body: Tube train drivers in the RMT union have called eight 24-hour strikes running over 16 days – including six in the lead-up to Christmas – that threaten to bring transport chaos to the capital. The drivers will start another series of 24-hour strikes in late November in opposition to plans for a four-day week, a proposal that has been warmly welcomed by the majority of London Underground drivers represented by the Aslef union. Disruption could mean few tube trains over the last shopping weekend before Christmas, with strikes running from noon on Thursday 17 December and again on Saturday 19 December. The 24-hour strikes will begin at noon on 26 November, followed by the Christmas industrial action, with two more strikes planned in early January and more in February.

items.title: A long-term Elon Musk backer is cashing out of Tesla — and cutting its SpaceX exposure
items.summary: Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust has cut its SpaceX holding to 11.1% of assets and sold its remaining Tesla stake.
items.body: A key early investor has sold the last of its Tesla shares and sharply reduced its SpaceX holding, taking profits from two of its most successful long-term bets. Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust , a London-listed closed-end fund managed by Baillie Gifford, said Friday that SpaceX represented 11.1% of its total assets as of Wednesday, down from 15% at Sept. 30. The position helped drive Scottish Mortgage's 31.5% net asset value return in the six months to the end of September. In its half-year results statement, Scottish Mortgage also said it sold its remaining Tesla stake in April, ending an investment that dated back to 2013. Scottish Mortgage first invested in SpaceX in December 2018, when Elon Musk 's rocket company had a reported valuation of about $31 billion, and committed roughly $200 million through 2021.

items.title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
items.summary: Investment has surged into the making of jet turbine blades - an extremely difficult component to make.
items.body: Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines. Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C. It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown. During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification. Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes.

items.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
items.summary: Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’ TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of…
items.body: TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model. Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”. The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.

items.title: Democratic sweep gives markets a reason to rethink path of interest rates
items.summary: Rate hikes could be curbed by an Iran war resolution, slower U.S. growth and fresh fiscal policy — but none are set in stone.
items.body: The Democrats' resounding victory in the U.S. midterms has the potential to curb interest rate hikes globally next year, according to market watchers — but the uncertain path of oil prices, U.S. economic growth and fiscal policies will be key. Central banks around the world are back in monetary tightening mode, with the Federal Reserve , Bank of England , European Central Bank and Bank of Japan all raising rates in recent months. The shift has in part stemmed from the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran driving up prices in oil and gas markets. The war has also exacerbated a squeeze in global refining capacity which has sent the cost of products like diesel, gasoline and jet fuel soaring.

items.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year to ramp Cybercab, Musk says
items.summary: The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales and Tesla has issued several voluntary recalls.
items.body: Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year. Musk , who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment , said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for manufacturing of its Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 .

items.title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
items.summary: Bad job interviews can be horrible to experience in the moment, but there is a lot they can teach us about the world of work
items.body: Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't. She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times". When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule. She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now. "I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff. Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable .

items.title: UK house prices fall at steepest rate in more than three years
items.summary: October drop of 0.6% leaves average price of property at £296,285, says Lloyds, as high mortgage rates hit market UK house prices fell at the steepest rate in more than three years in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline, as high mortgage rates hit the housing…
items.body: UK house prices fell at the steepest rate in more than three years in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline, as high mortgage rates hit the housing market. The average price of a typical UK property stood at £296,285 last month as prices unexpectedly dropped 0.6% compared with September, the steepest fall since the lender Lloyds recorded a 1.6% drop in August 2023. Analysts had expected a small monthly rise of 0.1%, which would have marked the first monthly increase since June. House prices were down 1.2% compared with the same month last year, the biggest annual fall since October 2023. “Housing demand is currently being tested by a challenging economic backdrop,” said Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds.

items.body: For years the “Christmas advert moment” has belonged to one brand. John Lewis’s syrupy commercials featuring piano ballads and tearjerker storylines have given the 160-year-old department store a cultural head start in the dash for festive profits. This year, however, there’s one high-street rival with a sackful of tricks to make up the ground. Marks & Spencer has brought out the big guns – in the form of a topless Santa, played by the small-screen heart-throb James Norton . The lively M&S Christmas ad has already drawn comparisons with John Lewis’s effort , which features Kristin Scott Thomas as a glamorous granny on the hunt to turn one room of her huge townhouse into a fun “gran cave”. items.title: AI stocks hammered by midterm shock as data center buildout becomes a 'war of attrition'
items.summary: The election rout landed on an AI trade already under pressure from high interest rates, heavy capital spending and questions about returns.
items.body: This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. The Democrats' stunning rout of the Republicans during the midterms this week wasn't just a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump , but also a potential roadblock to huge plans to build artificial intelligence data centers across the country. Since the landmark results came in, tech and AI stocks have been jolted by market volatility. The most valuable tech companies in the U.S. and Europe were hit with a massive sell-off on Thursday as investors got nervous. Nvidia lost 9.3%, with AMD shedding 17.3%, Microsoft 3.6%, Micron 17.5%, Broadcom 10.4%, Tesla 10.8% and SpaceX 9.1%. Neoclouds, which rely on their ability to serve AI computing power and are involved in massive data center projects, were also hit particularly hard.

items.title: Food bank to close amid rising costs
items.summary: A food bank in Goole annouces it will close in January as costs rise and donations drop.
items.body: A food bank serving an East Yorkshire town has closed after 16 years due to rising costs and a drop in donations. The Mission Trinity Food Bank, which supports people in Goole and the surrounding villages, began as part of the local Methodist church's mission to help homeless people and those facing financial hardship. Founder David Sample said: "Over time our funds have declined and declined, to the point where we can't really afford to keep going much longer, and also because of this cost of living crisis that's going on at the moment." He said the charity was buying in food up to three times a week to keep up with demand despite a drop in donations. "We've had to go out and buy more food with our funds, so we've been spending an awful lot more just to keep the basics in," he said.

items.title: US tech stock rout: is the AI bubble bursting?
items.summary: After Thursday’s share price plunge on Wall Street, could the volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown? Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections. This is not the first time stock markets…
items.body: After Thursday’s share price plunge on Wall Street, could the volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown? Global financial markets have been thrown into a tailspin as investors bet on an AI slowdown after the US midterm elections. This is not the first time stock markets have wobbled in recent months due to concerns over a tech bubble. But could this volatility be the start of a huge market meltdown? Shares on Wall Street plunged on Thursday , in a rout driven by AI and technology stocks that extended to Asia and Europe on Friday. US markets rebounded after trading reopened in New York, but failed to recover all of the lost ground amid lingering concerns of a relapse in selling pressure.

The council said more than 135,000 people have received support through its cost-of-living programmes, while more than £18.5m has been distributed to residents. items.title: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?
items.summary: With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans? More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week , with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe. What do we know so far, and…
items.body: More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week , with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe. At least 34 flights have been disrupted this week, beginning on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest. Thursday’s threats affected airports in London, Birmingham, Brussels, Bucharest, Madrid, Milan, Prague, Rome, Sofia and Warsaw, among others. So far all incidents have been confirmed to be false alarms, with nothing suspicious found by relevant security authorities. There is no clear pattern of airports and airlines targeted, although a significant number have involved Italian airports as an origin or destination. Seven flights this week were to – or from the UK – and four to or from Ireland.

items.title: AI debt concerns grow as ING reportedly seeks buyers for $500 million of data center loans
items.summary: ING is reportedly seeking bids for about $500 million across 12 data center loans, including debt tied to a New Mexico Stargate site.
items.body: ING is reportedly seeking buyers for a portfolio of 12 data center loans worth around $500 million, joining a broader push by banks to distribute credit risk tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out. The auction is said to include a $25 million piece linked to the Stargate project in New Mexico, which involves OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle , as well as certain other loan assets involving Vantage Data Centers and CyrusOne, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. ING will hold a bids-wanted-in-competition, or BWIC, auction process, with bids sized at $10 million or more due by Nov. 19, according to Bloomberg. A BWIC is a competitive process for investors to bid on pieces of a loan portfolio.

items.summary: People in Sussex say they are taking on extra work and not heating their homes due to oil prices.
items.body: A woman from East Sussex says she is having to take on extra work to pay for the soaring cost of her heating oil. Sheila Williams, from Golden Cross, has taken on a waitress job for the winter to help her pay her bills. She said her oil bill had doubled since the start of 2026 and the extra job was needed to help pay for it. A government spokesperson said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil and removed the 4% tariff on home heating oil." Williams, who has lived alone in a park home for seven years, said: "Words cannot express how upset I am about this." Thousands of homes across Sussex are not connected to the gas mains and rely on oil. A household wanting to fill a 1,000-litre tank could be facing a bill of more than £970 . Nigel Wanstall, from Sheffield Park, said: "We've no heating at all because I can't afford to fill my oil tank.

items.summary: Workers’ rights campaigners say measure will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay UK politics live – latest updates Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in an effort to empower both employees and…
items.body: Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in an effort to empower both employees and jobseekers. The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay. Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others . The prime minister said: “Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it. That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.

items.title: Oil prices tumble for the week as investors weigh Iran conflict risk after midterm elections
items.summary: Oil prices fell Friday as investors weighed the risk of renewed Iran war escalation after the midterms, alongside prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough.
items.body: Crude oil prices on Friday posted a steep weekly loss, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections. International benchmark Brent crude futures added 3 cents to close at $98.32 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 31 cents to settle at $90.83 per barrel. Brent fell more than 16% for the week while U.S. crude lost neary 13%. Investors are assessing whether the conclusion of the U.S. midterm elections could pave the way for renewed actions against Iran, potentially threatening oil supplies from the Middle East. Bob McNally, Rapidan Energy Group founder and president, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that he sees an 80% probability of military fighting resuming, forecasting that both oil benchmarks could climb above $100 a barrel.

items.body: An energy minister has told the bosses of Great Britain’s biggest energy suppliers to do more to help households get on top of their unpaid energy bills this winter, before the government spends up to £2.5bn to help write off the country’s record high debts. Energy bosses were summoned to a roundtable meeting on Thursday to discuss the government’s plan to pay down the energy debts of about 2.4m of the hardest-hit households. The debt relief scheme is part of a wider “circuit-breaker” strategy put forward by the chancellor in the annual budget statement last month. This includes measures to tackle household energy debt, which could reach £7bn by the end of the year.

items.title: Drones are changing warfare. But defense giants are still making billions from old-school weapons
items.summary: The world's biggest defense firms are finding that demand for traditional military equipment remains strong even as drones and AI reshape how wars are fought.
items.body: Drone technology and artificial intelligence are rapidly reshaping modern warfare, but the world's biggest defense contractors are finding that demand for tanks, fighter jets and other traditional military equipment remains strong. Recent earnings from U.S. and European defense companies show conventional weapons continue to drive year-on-year growth, even alongside surging demand for advanced sensors, autonomous systems and counter-drone technology. Rather than displacing traditional weapons manufacturers, the rise of drones and autonomous warfare is creating new business for many of the same companies. From counter-drone defenses to advanced sensors integrated into tanks and fighter jets, the technologies transforming the battlefield are also changing, or even expanding, the markets served by legacy defense giants.

items.body: Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 10.44%, while Samsung Electronics shed 6.35%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 7.02% and 4.45%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector. The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure. I n Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 4.99%, while Tokyo Electron slid over 5%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 10.83%.

items.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis
items.summary: Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in…
items.body: Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days. At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers. Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests. In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

items.body: The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede. McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively. Oil prices had spiked above the $100 mark ahead of the midterm elections as investors weighed uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict and the risk of further U.S. military actions.

items.title: Fearing AI disruption, white-collar workers are quitting their jobs
items.summary: While there’s no evidence linking AI to mass layoffs, the tech has already ‘changed worker psychology’ When artificial intelligence researcher Mrinank Sharma quit his job at Anthropic earlier this year, the news rippled across the internet. In his resignation letter, posted on X…
items.body: W hen artificial intelligence researcher Mrinank Sharma quit his job at Anthropic earlier this year, the news rippled across the internet. In his resignation letter, posted on X and viewed 15.3m times, Sharma warned of a world “in peril” from the technology he had helped build. “It is clear to me the time has come to move on,” he wrote. His next move: a poetry degree. In the months following Sharma’s resignation, AI industry defectors and workers outside of Silicon Valley alike have echoed his sentiments. Bracing for disruption forecasted by the AI industry, white-collar professionals are voluntarily leaving established careers to pursue professions they feel are more secure or more aligned with their values. Workers across industries – from tech to public relations to consulting – say AI changed the substance and stability of their jobs overnight.

items.title: ‘Every day, someone loses a hand or a leg’: the brutal reality of India’s textile recycling industry
items.summary: In Panipat, 1m tons of used clothing a year are turned into products for global brands, but dangerous machinery and few safeguards mean life-changing injuries are common For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an…
items.body: F or three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world. Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms. “I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them.

items.body: L inda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry. In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump . She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House. But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year.

items.body: Equinix says its smaller data centers could be less exposed to potential U.S. construction restrictions as regulators scrutinize the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company's facilities typically range from 30 to 60 megawatts, compared with the roughly 100-megawatt threshold that Cyrus Adaggra, Equinix's Asia-Pacific president, said is generally targeted by U.S. proposals. His comments come as the U.S. midterm election results have heightened concerns that new restrictions on data center development could delay projects and raise construction costs. items.title: Jim Cramer says the AI sell-off isn't over, but it isn't another dot-com crash
items.summary: Cramer warned that the sell-off in AI stocks likely has further to run.
items.body: The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC's Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic. Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron tumbled 17%, GE Vernova dropped 7% and Sandisk plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday's session. "I wish I could say that today's flush was the bottom," the " Mad Money " host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn't believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today's AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.

items.title: In Focus: Salmon disappearing as Japan's catch just 3% of 2003 peak
items.body: ABASHIRI/SHIBETSU, Japan -- Salmon catches in Hokkaido this autumn totaled just under 6,000 tons as of late October, only 3% of the 2003 peak. Fishermen are not only worried about poor catches this year, they are also agonizing over "whether they can continue salmon fishing," said Tetsuya Shinya, head of the Abashiri Fisheries Cooperative. Locals have long taken it for granted that salmon return to their natal streams and rivers. "Hokkaido has benefitted from salmon over more than 10,000 years," said Masaki Ichimura, director of the Shibetsu Salmon Museum. In addition to humans, wild animals in the forests, such as brown bears and foxes, have survived harsh winters due to the nutrition provided by salmon. Though salmon might be familiar to humans, there are still have many secrets to unlock about their behavior. Juvenile salmon swim from freshwater rivers down to the ocean.
